tEn: From Microsoft to Startup: Gary's Journey and the Cult of Earnestness
tZh: 从微软到创业：Gary 的旅程与真诚的信徒
sEn: Gary shares his early career mistakes, the importance of earnestness over hype, and why startups must be like cults to succeed.
sZh: Gary 分享了他早期的职业错误、真诚胜过炒作的重要性，以及为什么初创公司必须像邪教一样才能成功。

consensus.en: Earnestness and courage are essential for founders; follow your own direct experience rather than what's hot.
consensus.zh: 真诚和勇气对创始人至关重要；要遵循自己的直接经验，而不是追逐热门。

consensus.en: The future is already here, not evenly distributed; first-principles knowledge and direct experience reveal secret truths.
consensus.zh: 未来已经到来，只是分布不均；第一性原理知识和直接经验能揭示秘密真理。

consensus.en: AI and agentic coding enable individuals to become multiples of themselves, making founders more ambitious than ever.
consensus.zh: AI和智能体式编码使个人能力倍增，让创始人比以往任何时候都更有雄心。

consensus.en: Markdown files and skills are becoming employees; business processes can be automated into reusable, perfect loops.
consensus.zh: Markdown文件和技能正成为员工；业务流程可自动化成可复用、完美的循环。

consensus.en: Society and companies are slower to change than expected; this is a white pill, not a bad thing.
consensus.zh: 社会和公司的变化比预期慢；这是一颗白色药丸，不是坏事。

consensus.en: Local action and civic engagement are crucial; fixing local issues can fix state and national problems.
consensus.zh: 本地行动和公民参与至关重要；解决本地问题可以解决州和国家的问题。

contrarian.en: The most interesting things often start as toys or fringe ideas, not obviously important ones.
contrarian.zh: 最有趣的事物往往始于玩具或边缘想法，而非显然重要的事物。

contrarian.en: Pure per-seat SaaS may not exist in 5-10 years; it's only a wedge, not a moat.
contrarian.zh: 纯按席位收费的SaaS在5-10年内可能不复存在；它只是楔子，不是护城河。

contrarian.en: The mid-level of bureaucracy should be agents, not humans; management layers can be automated.
contrarian.zh: 中层官僚机构应该由智能体而非人类担任；管理层可以被自动化。

contrarian.en: AI erases the API line; even bug reports can be handled by agents, enabling back-and-forth.
contrarian.zh: AI抹平了API线；甚至错误报告也能由智能体处理，实现双向互动。

contrarian.en: The slowness of bureaucracy and human limitations are actually a white pill, not doom.
contrarian.zh: 官僚主义的缓慢和人类的局限性实际上是白色药丸，而非厄运。

contrarian.en: Government and institutions are not ready for agents; but they won't be replaced quickly, which is good.
contrarian.zh: 政府和机构尚未为智能体做好准备；但它们不会很快被取代，这是好事。

turns.zh: 而且它还没有准备好。它还没有为智能体能以光速思考的世界做好准备。就像你有无限量的它，无限量的数据。然后，你知道，我的希望是基本上产品会好上 10 倍或 100 倍。它们应该好上一千倍。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Like services should be a thousand times better, right? Like you know, the invisible hand of capitalism at that point, if properly done, it's not about lowering the cost of something. It should actually be creating these sort of magical things. Like I was on Wall Street Journal podcast recently and the reporter kept trying to gotcha me. He kept saying, 'Are you guys in tech trying to make a utopia?' And I was like, this is a trap. I would not go so far as to say that, but as I went through a bunch of examples from a bunch of the startups that you and I have worked on and funded and things like that, I was like, actually maybe, right? You know, we may never achieve a utopia, but it is worthy and worth it to attempt, right? And I would not say that Silicon Valley or tech will achieve a utopia. I will very earnestly say that we are trying to bring about a better world.
turns.zh: 就像服务应该好上一千倍，对吧？你知道，资本主义的无形之手在那个时候，如果做得好，就不是关于降低某物的成本。它实际上应该创造这些神奇的东西。比如我最近上了《华尔街日报》的播客，记者一直试图让我难堪。他不停地说：“你们科技界是在试图创造一个乌托邦吗？”我当时想，这是个陷阱。我不会说得那么远，但当我列举了你和我一起工作过、资助过的一堆初创公司的例子时，我想，实际上也许吧，对吧？你知道，我们可能永远无法实现乌托邦，但尝试是值得的，对吧？而且我不会说硅谷或科技界会实现乌托邦。我会非常诚恳地说，我们正在努力带来一个更美好的世界。

turns.en: Maybe another way to say this is just this is the least happy you'll ever be.
turns.zh: 也许另一种说法是，这是你最不快乐的时刻。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: You know, because I think one of the other implications of what you're describing is just the ergonomics of the sort of white-collar job today. You know, you think about every—you've worked at big companies. Like you think of just the kind of morass that you have to get through.
turns.zh: 你知道，因为我认为你所描述的另一个含义就是如今白领工作的人体工程学。你知道，你想想每一个——你在大公司工作过。就像你想想你必须穿越的那种泥潭。

turns.en: Torture.
turns.zh: 折磨。

turns.en: You think of how lossy the communication is. Like the entire management science, sort of managerial class. Like maybe that was a 100-year distraction from what was founder mode, you know, from the Industrial Revolution all the way through Henry Ford, all the way through some of the early Silicon Valley founders, and then everybody just kind of hit this tidal wave of management.
turns.zh: 你想想沟通的损耗有多大。就像整个管理科学，那种管理阶层。也许那是从创始人模式中分心的一百年，你知道，从工业革命一直到亨利·福特，一直到一些早期的硅谷创始人，然后每个人都遇到了这股管理的浪潮。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。

turns.en: Now we have this new model that can lead to dramatic productivity improvements, like 3 days a week of really intentional work. Maybe 1 day.
turns.zh: 现在我们有了这个新模型，可以带来巨大的生产力提升，比如每周 3 天的真正专注工作。也许 1 天。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And the other days you're touching grass. And I think the time that you do spend is just so much less burdened by this stuff that you always felt like you had to wade through.
turns.zh: 而其他日子你在接触草地。我认为你实际花费的时间会少很多负担，不再总是觉得必须费力穿过这些东西。

turns.en: Yeah, that's right. I mean, if you look at the typical Mag 7 day-to-day, it's insane. Like I remember when I was 22 working on Windows Mobile. We were working on these crazy devices that were like years before the iPhone. And we needed integration, for instance, from the Windows team, which was on the other side of the highway in Redmond.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我的意思是，如果你看看典型的 Mag 7 的日常，那太疯狂了。我记得我 22 岁时在 Windows Mobile 团队工作。我们在开发这些疯狂的设备，比 iPhone 早了好几年。我们需要集成，比如来自 Windows 团队，他们在雷德蒙德高速公路的另一边。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And then I remember, me and my sort of PM mentor, we had to go over to the Windows team and they wouldn't reply to our emails. They wouldn't fix our bugs. They wouldn't even mark it as won't fix. They just ignored us. And we had to go over there with a baseball bat. Like I don't know why he brought one. It wasn't like he was going to rough anyone up. It was just like this vague threat or something. It was actually hilarious and I think about that all the time. It's like what kind of bureaucratic hell is it where two perfectly smart people who are making good tech money are put into a situation where there's a fiefdom over here. Literally there's like seven levels between us and that person.
turns.zh: 然后我记得，我和我的项目经理导师，我们不得不去 Windows 团队那边，他们不回我们的邮件。他们不修复我们的 bug。他们甚至不标记为“不会修复”。他们就是无视我们。我们不得不带着棒球棒过去。我不知道他为什么带了一根。他不是要去揍谁。那只是一个模糊的威胁之类的。实际上那很搞笑，我经常想起这件事。这就像什么样的官僚地狱，两个非常聪明、赚着高薪技术钱的人，被置于一个这里有封地的情况。实际上我们和那个人之间有七层。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And this person doesn't even know that we spent like four hours trying to get a P3 bug fix that was a blocker for a thousand of our users or something.
turns.zh: 而这个人甚至不知道我们花了四个小时试图修复一个 P3 错误，那是一个阻碍我们一千个用户的问题。

turns.en: And how much humanity is just wasted?
turns.zh: 有多少人性就这样被浪费了？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: How many 2:00 a.m. sort of anxious wake-ups were there because somebody wanted to not have a hard conversation? Like it's a really a waste of the way we should be spending our time in working.
turns.zh: 有多少次凌晨两点的焦虑醒来，是因为有人不想进行艰难的对话？这真的是对我们工作时间的浪费。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And that's a profound version of like the seven plus or minus two. Like I don't think that the product unit manager or whatever their title was wanted us to waste our time like that. I think it's just that your day, you just don't have enough hours in the day and we're incredibly limited human beings.
turns.zh: 而这是七加减二的深刻版本。我不认为产品单元经理或不管他们的头衔是什么，想要我们那样浪费时间。我认为只是你的日子，你一天没有足够的时间，而我们是非常有限的人类。

turns.en: But you know, yeah, it's funny. I think about my time at Microsoft and it's like I remember getting an iPod and doing competitive research for Windows Mobile versus the iPod. I can imagine today at Microsoft you can imagine a markdown file and a skill that is run on a cron.
turns.zh: 但你知道，是的，这很有趣。我想起我在微软的时光，我记得拿到一个 iPod，为 Windows Mobile 与 iPod 做竞争研究。我可以想象今天在微软，你可以想象一个 markdown 文件和一个按计划任务运行的技能。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And it's like, how are all the people working on this team? Are they blocked? Who are they blocked by? What are the external dependencies? Like suddenly there is a graph, there's a loop, and then suddenly the products can actually just move. You could release something in a day or two that would have taken like 6 months. It's incredible. And if you could multiply that out across the org, like Microsoft probably can't.
turns.zh: 然后就像，这个团队的所有人怎么样？他们被阻塞了吗？他们被谁阻塞？外部依赖是什么？就像突然有一个图，有一个循环，然后突然产品实际上就能动了。你可以在一天或两天内发布一些东西，而以前需要 6 个月。这太不可思议了。如果你能在整个组织中推广，像微软可能做不到。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: But a startup can.
turns.zh: 但初创公司可以。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And every startup must.
turns.zh: 而且每个初创公司都必须这样做。

turns.en: Yes, they must be organized as well. I also love what you said, it's almost like the mid-level of bureaucracy should be agents. Because I actually think that being in charge is somewhat overstated. I love to actually have at least the mid-level organize the work, resolve the conflicts that it can somewhat programmatically, probabilistically programmatically. Of course, the executive team maybe sets direction, the individual sort of decides on execution, but just the whole organization layer, which a lot of product managers historically did, should not be human.
turns.zh: 是的，他们必须组织良好。我也喜欢你所说的，几乎就像中层官僚机构应该是智能体。因为我实际上认为掌权有点被高估了。我实际上希望至少中层来组织工作，解决它可以以某种编程方式、概率编程方式解决的冲突。当然，执行团队可能设定方向，个人决定执行，但整个组织层，历史上很多产品经理做的，不应该由人类来做。

turns.en: I mean, the great thing is it doesn't have to be. You know how Venkatesh Rao has this thing where it's like, you need to be above the API line? Like if Uber came out, if you're an Uber driver, you're below the API line. You should be fighting to be above the API line. I actually think AI erases the API line. One of the funniest things I saw recently is there's an API company that we funded called Kolabtree, and they released a bug report endpoint that is not for humans to use, it's for agents who use their software to use. And there's an LLM where if there's a bug in the software, the bug report goes, but then it replies real time.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，最棒的是它不必如此。你知道 Venkatesh Rao 有个说法，就是你要在 API 线之上吗？比如 Uber 出现了，如果你是 Uber 司机，你就在 API 线之下。你应该努力站到 API 线之上。我其实认为 AI 会抹平 API 线。我最近看到的最有趣的事情之一是，我们投资的一家 API 公司叫 Kolabtree，他们发布了一个 bug 报告端点，不是给人用的，而是给使用他们软件的智能体用的。有一个 LLM，如果软件有 bug，bug 报告会发过去，然后它会实时回复。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And it's like, actually, that's a good bug, we filed it, we're going to fix it next week, but also try this workaround.
turns.zh: 然后它就像，实际上，这是个好 bug，我们已记录，下周会修复，但也可以试试这个变通方案。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: And then I can't get that out of my head because you could imagine that could be how companies work, right? Instead of being below the API line and having to do what the API tells you to do.
turns.zh: 然后我就一直忘不掉这个，因为你可以想象，这可能就是公司运作的方式，对吧？而不是在 API 线之下，不得不做 API 告诉你的事。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Like this can be a back and forth actually.
turns.zh: 实际上，这可以是一个来回的互动。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And then I always think about the reason why cars in the '80s got so good in Japan was actually a management technique. They realized the Toyota production system meant that if you are the person doing the work on the line, you should be allowed to change the line because you are the person with the most amount of contacts to be able to improve your own working situation. And that's why American cars really started sucking and why Japanese cars became absolutely incredible. It's this very subtle simple way that actually empowers the worker. So there's a sort of mix that I think is interesting.
turns.zh: 然后我总会想到，80 年代日本汽车变得这么好的原因，其实是一种管理技巧。他们意识到丰田生产系统意味着，如果你是流水线上干活的人，你应该被允许改变流水线，因为你是拥有最多接触点的人，能够改善自己的工作状况。这就是为什么美国汽车开始变得很烂，而日本汽车变得绝对出色。这是一种非常微妙简单的方式，实际上赋予了工人权力。所以我觉得有一种混合是很有趣的。

turns.en: Interesting, because what's traditionally seen as a hierarchical society came up with this very bottom-up way of working which led to arguably a 40-year generational run because of process power.
turns.zh: 有趣，因为传统上被视为等级森严的社会，却提出了这种非常自下而上的工作方式，这可以说带来了 40 年的代际繁荣，因为流程的力量。

turns.en: Yeah. Which is beautiful.
turns.zh: 是的。这很美好。

turns.zh: 你觉得这些问题中有多少是受智能限制的？比如我们需要更聪明的模型，还是会有其他模型属性来解锁成功？

turns.en: I mean, honestly, it's all human.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，说实话，都是人类。

turns.en: Uh
turns.zh: 呃

turns.en: Humans are the ones who are going to slow this down.
turns.zh: 人类才是会拖慢这一切的人。

turns.en: And then
turns.zh: 然后

turns.en: Actually I'm realizing this might be a white pill.
turns.zh: 实际上我意识到这可能是一颗白丸。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: So if you look at the tenor of what's going on just broadly in the discourse about AI, it's all this sort of doom and gloom, like all white-collar jobs are going to go away. There's going to be a permanent underclass.
turns.zh: 所以如果你看看关于 AI 的广泛讨论的基调，都是这种悲观论调，比如所有白领工作都会消失。将会有一个永久的底层阶级。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And then funny enough, what I think is all of the bureaucracy and the slowness and the seven plus or minus two of every company, every institution, every organization, all the middle managers in the world.
turns.zh: 然后有趣的是，我认为所有的官僚主义、缓慢，以及每家公司、每个机构、每个组织的七加减二，世界上所有的中层管理者。

turns.en: Uh
turns.zh: 呃

turns.en: That is actually the white pill.
turns.zh: 那实际上是白丸。

turns.en: So you know these things are going to be slower than you think.
turns.zh: 所以你知道这些事情会比你想的更慢。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Right? I looked at, you know, we had 7,000 people. Most of them were 18 to 22 years old.
turns.zh: 对吧？我看了看，你知道，我们有 7000 人。他们大多数是 18 到 22 岁。

turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.en: And I looked in their faces and they're all AI native. They were born more or less, you know, they became adults in the time of ChatGPT.
turns.zh: 我看着他们的脸，他们都是 AI 原生代。他们出生时差不多，你知道，他们在 ChatGPT 时代成年。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And it's going to, you know, and for us it's like now we run, which is nice.
turns.zh: 而且这会，你知道，对我们来说，现在我们掌权，这很好。

turns.en: That's great, right?
turns.zh: 那太好了，对吧？

turns.en: But, you know, imagine us like 20 years ago. We were the ones who were native to the web. We were the ones who were native to mobile. And then now we run, so all of society runs on the things that we expected from when we were 18 to 22. So I think that the white pill to me is like it's going to be 20 years and that's not a bad thing. That's actually a good thing.
turns.zh: 但是，你知道，想象我们 20 年前。我们是网络原生代。我们是移动原生代。然后现在我们掌权，所以整个社会都运行在我们 18 到 22 岁时所期待的东西上。所以我认为，对我来说，白丸就是这需要 20 年，这不是坏事。这实际上是好事。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Society is way slower than you think. Government is way slower than you think. Every company in the world is way slower than you think.
turns.zh: 社会比你想的慢得多。政府比你想的慢得多。世界上每家公司都比你想的慢得多。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And there are real moats to these things. There are structural reasons why a Microsoft isn't going anywhere.
turns.zh: 而且这些事情有真正的护城河。微软不会消失是有结构性原因的。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And then I guess this is sort of a little antithetical to what most people in Silicon Valley would say like, "I want to start up to replace all of them."
turns.zh: 然后我想这有点与硅谷大多数人会说的相反，比如“我想创业取代他们所有人。”

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And the reality is like they won't, you know?
turns.zh: 而现实是他们不会，你知道吧？

turns.en: They won't. I love it. Okay, I have two more questions for you. One on this kind of sort of trying to envision the near future, what do you think the next computer looks like? What does a new computer look like?
turns.zh: 他们不会。我喜欢这个。好的，我还有两个问题要问你。一个是关于设想近期未来的，你觉得下一代电脑会是什么样子？新电脑会是什么样子？

turns.en: Oh, man. I think in the short term it'll probably keep looking like the way it is, but it seems inconceivable that it'll stay that form factor. It's pretty clearly going to be voice.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。我认为短期内它可能还会保持现在的样子，但似乎难以想象它会一直保持那种形态。很明显会是语音。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: I think there's a lot around memory. It's going to take a while to, you know, we're at this moment where everyone's sort of happy with ChatGPT or Claude Co-work or whatever it is.
turns.zh: 我认为在记忆方面有很多。这需要一段时间，你知道，我们现在处于每个人都对 ChatGPT 或 Claude Co-work 之类的感到满意的时刻。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: But I don't think they will be in the long term. I think you're going to want a lot more context, and you're going to want like all watched over by machines of living grace. You're going to want this thing that is benevolent, knows about your hopes, fears, and desires, and then is sort of relentlessly searching to help you in that way. And that's actually going to be really exciting. And you know, the path through that will probably be like computer use, memory, like diarization, like ingestion, like yeah, I mean I think there's going to be a lot there.
turns.zh: 但我认为长期来看不会。我认为你会想要更多的上下文，你会想要像“被优雅的机器所注视”那样的东西。你会想要这个东西是仁慈的，知道你的希望、恐惧和欲望，然后不懈地以那种方式帮助你。那实际上会非常令人兴奋。而且你知道，实现这一点的路径可能会是电脑使用、记忆、说话人分离、信息摄取之类的，是的，我认为那里会有很多。

turns.en: And you know, the cool thing is it's actually going to take longer. Like, this isn't a, I don't think people are even talking about this now. My guess is like next year, 2027, will be like the harness wars.
turns.zh: 而且你知道，酷的是这实际上需要更长时间。比如，这不是一个，我觉得人们现在甚至还没在谈论这个。我猜明年，2027 年，会是“套件之战”。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: You know, and then but it's really a cost thing. It's just too expensive right now.
turns.zh: 你知道，然后但这真的是成本问题。现在太贵了。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: You know? But it won't be. There will be a war for a billion consumers.
turns.zh: 你知道吧？但不会一直这样。将会有一场争夺十亿消费者的战争。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Right when the frontier pure model compute of today will be like maybe 50 or 100 bucks in like two or three years.
turns.zh: 就在今天的前沿纯模型算力在两三年后可能只要 50 或 100 美元的时候。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And then that will be when the browser wars will be back on.
turns.zh: 然后那将是浏览器大战重新开始的时候。

turns.en: Yes. Yes. Well, we're already seeing it like the price per token of frontier is going to infinity. My thesis is infinity dollars a token, you can't have it. And the price per token of the model that was frontier a week ago is collapsing to zero.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。我们已经看到了，前沿模型的每 token 价格正在走向无穷大。我的论点是每 token 无穷美元，你无法拥有它。而一周前还是前沿的模型，其每 token 价格正在崩溃到零。

turns.en: And I actually think to me that is a huge white pill for a lot of reasons. You know, one of the most important of which is just we need more consumer AI software. And in a world where most consumer products are free to try, you just can't do that when you have really high costs of incremental distribution. The magic of software is zero cost incremental distribution. We have these magical primitives. Like, we have computers that are emotive and have emotional texture for the first time in 40 or 50 years. What a tragedy that we haven't built more ambitious consumer products yet.
turns.zh: 而且我实际上认为，对我来说，这是一个巨大的白丸，原因有很多。你知道，其中最重要的一点就是我们确实需要更多的消费级 AI 软件。在一个大多数消费产品都可以免费试用的世界里，如果增量分发成本很高，你就没法做到这一点。软件的魔力在于零成本的增量分发。我们拥有这些神奇的原始构件。比如，我们有了情感丰富、带有情绪质感的电脑，这是四五十年来头一回。我们还没有打造出更有雄心的消费产品，这真是个悲剧。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: So, I'm really excited for this sort of changing economics of models to unlock these new categories.
turns.zh: 所以，我真的很兴奋，模型经济学的这种变化能解锁这些新的品类。

turns.en: I mean and we're so early. Like I was convinced that like being becoming a convert to open claw made me very very convinced that it was going to happen right away and then at this point I'm like that's not correct at all. Like
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我们还太早了。就像我确信，成为 open claw 的皈依者让我非常非常确信它会马上发生，但到了这个时候，我觉得那完全不对。就像……

turns.en: Yeah. Well, you should try the new chat GPT desktop app actually has got a voice mode and it's sort of it's an operator or a concierge that can see all your threads.
turns.zh: 是啊。嗯，你应该试试新的 ChatGPT 桌面应用，它实际上有语音模式，有点像操作员或礼宾员，能看到你所有的对话线程。

turns.en: Oh, cool.
turns.zh: 哦，酷。

turns.en: And you can access it from your phone. It's very open claw-ish and I'm sure Peter had his hands all over it. To me it's the closest thing we've seen yet to a true consumer assistant.
turns.zh: 而且你可以从手机上访问它。它非常 open claw 风格，我确信 Peter 在其中投入了大量心血。对我来说，这是我们迄今为止见过的最接近真正消费级助手的东西。

turns.en: Oh, I can see it's awesome.
turns.zh: 哦，我看得出来，太棒了。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Chat GPT always had like basically the best memory. So I got to try it again.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。ChatGPT 基本上一直拥有最好的记忆。所以我得再试试。

turns.en: They've done a great job.
turns.zh: 他们做得很好。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: Okay, last question you know, we talked a lot about kind of utopian visions for the world and problems that are maybe intelligence bound. You've also put a lot of energy into sort of local politics and doing things I think are very pro-social, but it seems like more of those problems are human coordination bound.
turns.zh: 好的，最后一个问题。你知道，我们谈了很多关于世界的乌托邦愿景，以及那些可能受智能限制的问题。你也投入了很多精力在地方政治上，做了一些我认为非常亲社会的事情，但似乎更多这类问题是受人类协作限制的。

turns.en: Oh, definitely.
turns.zh: 哦，绝对是。

turns.en: Yeah, how do you get energy to do that work? You know, is there a white pill for that aspect of our society? Maybe talk a bit about that.
turns.zh: 是啊，你如何获得精力去做那项工作？你知道，对我们社会的这一方面，有白丸吗？也许谈谈这个。

turns.en: I mean the white pill is just believing that America still has rule of law and that people in government are trying to help and like somewhat earnest. Like it's not perfect. I think that the white pill for me recently was even just doing jury duty in San Francisco and to see like this orderly process of really a cross-section of San Francisco. One thing I realized was like actually we are a big part of the city. Like we're 10 20% of the people are like directly working in tech.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，白丸就是相信美国仍然有法治，政府中的人们在努力提供帮助，而且有点真诚。就像它并不完美。我认为最近对我来说的白丸，甚至只是在旧金山履行陪审团义务，看到这样一个有序的过程，真正是旧金山的一个横截面。我意识到的一件事是，实际上我们是这座城市的重要组成部分。就像我们占 10% 到 20% 的人口，直接从事科技工作。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: And so um to see something that was I mean the judge was really good. I mean it was a horrible case, but like you know, government is not here to like ruin people. Like
turns.zh: 所以，嗯，看到一些东西，我的意思是法官真的很好。我的意思是那是一个可怕的案件，但你知道，政府不是来毁掉人们的。就像……

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: And so and then at that point um we can vote.
turns.zh: 所以，然后在那时，嗯，我们可以投票。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Like we actually have a say and then I think everything is downstream of media at that point. Like I think the San Francisco moment that got me very engaged was realizing you know Asian Americans are 25% of the voting populace about 30% of the population but during COVID like we had a district attorney who was turning a blind eye to some of the most heinous crimes against our elders and simultaneous to that we had a school board that was openly hostile against Asian American kids who just wanted to learn algebra in public middle school which hit me because I was that public school kid in Fremont in the East Bay. Like if I couldn't have taken algebra in middle school, I couldn't take calculus by senior year. I wouldn't have been able to study engineering at Stanford and I wouldn't be here doing any of the things I get to do today and I'm like oh okay now now they've made it personal and like let me understand and it turned out to be like sort of all the same people the same people who want to destroy all the data same people who don't want to build any housing in anywhere in California or the world. Like it's sort of Nimbys who want to virtue signal who sort of have these ideologies that like don't square with mine. I mean as a builder you like well you know words have meaning like supply and demand exists markets exist like incentives exist and then you know I think that government is what you know when people like us don't speak up when we don't like pay attention and like hold our media accountable not just the government then things get very deranged and that's what San Francisco was I think around COVID and then just by sheer organization like this is I think that like the Chinese of the West Side organizing around algebra and you know the deaths of our elders going to farmers markets and like literally physically like telling each other they're killing us and they're killing us right um ABC News you know literally the meat the mainstream media TV channel of San Francisco and the Bay Area would not cover anti-Chinese and anti-Asian crime. And you know I I it's like unconscionable right like our institutions failed us and the great thing is like when the system becomes so odious you've got to put your body on it. I think that was Mario Savio. And it's kind of I mean it's ironic almost to like say that but on the other hand like that's what I believe like they can't do this to us and we're going to stop it. And even at like personal peril even at you know reputational cost like we should be willing to take that cost because that's our covenant with our fellow man and our fellow citizen you know and if we don't do it who's going to do it like nobody does it and I'm super proud of what we're doing in San Francisco because we have beat back that ideological set of people who like created this mess and you know it's not perfect in San Francisco but it's getting better.
turns.zh: 就像我们实际上有发言权，然后我认为那时一切都取决于媒体。就像我认为让我非常投入的旧金山时刻，是意识到你知道亚裔美国人占投票人口的 25%，约占人口的 30%，但在新冠疫情期间，我们有一位地区检察官对针对我们长者的最令人发指的罪行视而不见，与此同时，我们有一个学校董事会公开敌视那些只想在公立中学学习代数的亚裔美国孩子，这让我很受触动，因为我就是东湾弗里蒙特的那个公立学校孩子。就像如果我不能在中学学代数，我就不能在高三学微积分。我就不能去斯坦福学工程，也就不会在这里做我今天能做的任何事情，然后我想，哦，好吧，现在他们让这件事变得个人化了，让我来理解一下，结果发现，就像都是同一群人，那些想摧毁所有数据的人，那些不想在加州或世界任何地方建造任何住房的人。就像那些想炫耀道德优越感的 NIMBY 主义者，他们有一些与我不相符的意识形态。我的意思是，作为一个建设者，你会说，你知道，词语有意义，供需存在，市场存在，激励存在，然后你知道，我认为政府是，你知道，当我们这样的人不发声，当我们不注意，不追究媒体的责任，而不仅仅是政府时，事情就会变得非常混乱，我认为旧金山在新冠期间就是这样，然后仅仅通过纯粹的组织，我认为这就像西边的华人围绕代数和我们长者的死亡组织起来，去农贸市场，像字面上身体力行地告诉彼此，他们在杀害我们，他们在杀害我们，嗯，ABC 新闻，你知道，字面上，旧金山和湾区的主流媒体电视频道，不会报道反华和反亚裔的犯罪。你知道，我，这真是违背良心，对吧，我们的机构辜负了我们，而伟大之处在于，当系统变得如此可憎时，你必须把身体压上去。我认为那是马里奥·萨维奥说的。而且这有点，我的意思是，说这个几乎有点讽刺，但另一方面，这就是我相信的，他们不能这样对我们，我们要阻止它。即使冒着个人危险，即使你知道要付出声誉代价，我们也应该愿意承担这个代价，因为这是我们与同胞和公民的契约，你知道，如果我们不做，谁来做？没有人做，我为我们在旧金山所做的事情感到非常自豪，因为我们已经击退了那些制造了这场混乱的意识形态人群，你知道，旧金山并不完美，但它正在变得更好。

turns.en: It's amazing right now.
turns.zh: 现在真是太棒了。

turns.en: I mean I think I saw that Lori might be the most popular mayor or politician in the entire country. Yeah. Things have gotten so much better. Everybody sees it feels it in the vibe. Some people say I wonder why but I think for those of us who know we see that your sort of stewardship not just of the industry of the startup community of sort of technology but also of the community is one of the big catalysts. So thank you for doing that work.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我想我看到 Lori 可能是全国最受欢迎的市长或政治家。是的。事情已经好多了。每个人都能看到，能在氛围中感受到。有些人说我想知道为什么，但我认为对于我们这些了解的人来说，我们看到你不仅对行业、创业社区、技术，而且对社区的管理是重要的催化剂之一。所以感谢你做那项工作。

turns.en: Thank you so much. Yeah. So and I think San Francisco should be the beacon for pushing this back in every blue city in America as you know I that's what Gary's list.org is basically like how do we take the lessons that we learned here and like LA needs this, New York needs this, Minneapolis needs this, Seattle needs this.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。是的。所以，我认为旧金山应该成为在美国每个蓝城推动这种反击的灯塔，你知道，这就是 Gary's list.org 的基本内容，我们如何把在这里学到的经验教训，洛杉矶需要这个，纽约需要这个，明尼阿波利斯需要这个，西雅图需要这个。

turns.en: Well, and also let's find you know to connect the two that sort of you know culture society and technology like let's find very local ways for the ambition that this technology unlocks to show up. You know, I was in London last week and you were talking a little bit what's possible. It's like hey, you don't have to have an American vision for how AI impacts your society. If you want the NHS to be incredible then like you can do that with this technology.
turns.zh: 嗯，而且让我们找到，你知道，连接这两者，那种你知道的文化、社会和技术，让我们找到非常本地化的方式，让这项技术解锁的雄心得以展现。你知道，我上周在伦敦，你谈了一点什么是可能的。就像，嘿，你不必对美国 AI 如何影响你的社会有一个美国愿景。如果你想让 NHS 变得不可思议，那么你可以用这项技术做到。

turns.en: So the opportunity for ambition to be very localized in our communities is something I think is really interesting.
turns.zh: 所以，野心在社区中本地化的机会，我觉得真的很有意思。

turns.en: Yeah, and so act local, like take care of the people right next to you. You know, I think it's funny—so many people get very, very obsessed with national. I mean, we want to look at national generally right now. It's like, you know what? I care about San Francisco, I care about housing, I care about crime, I care about treatment and recovery.
turns.zh: 是的，所以要本地行动，比如照顾好你身边的人。你知道，我觉得很有趣——很多人对全国层面非常非常着迷。我的意思是，我们现在通常想关注全国。但你知道吗？我关心旧金山，我关心住房，我关心犯罪，我关心治疗和康复。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And if we do that, like we can have the society we want to live in. And then, you know, if we fix local, like state and national will fix itself, because on a five or ten year basis, the people who win up there will come up through a system that's functional and about saying no to things that don't make sense, about saying yes to the things that are awesome for the people.
turns.zh: 如果我们这样做，我们就能拥有我们想要生活的社会。然后，你知道，如果我们解决了本地问题，州和全国层面就会自我修复，因为在五到十年的基础上，那些在上面获胜的人会通过一个功能正常的系统脱颖而出，这个系统会对不合理的事情说不，对人民有益的事情说是。

turns.en: I love it. All right, Gary. First of many. Thanks, brother.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。好的，Gary，这只是第一次，以后还有很多次。谢谢，兄弟。

turns.en: Thanks, bro.
turns.zh: 谢谢，兄弟。

turns.en: This is great.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。

turns.en: Cool. Yeah.
turns.zh: 酷，是的。
